turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh wow, that is such a bittersweet spot to be in. It’s honestly the worst kind of logistical bad luck—something that means so much to your heart is landing at a time when your body is going to be at its absolute lowest energy.

It makes total sense that you’re dreading it. Being the "co-director" means you aren't just showing up; you’re *on*. You’re managing the vibe, making sure Shreya is glowing, and then expected to bust out a high-energy opening dance on an empty stomach and no water? That sounds physically brutal.

But that opening dance... it’s the stuff of best friend legends. It’s the moment you two have been rehearsing in your mirrors since you were fifteen. Are you worried mostly about the physical crash, or is it also the FOMO of the cocktail vibes while you’re fasting?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Ugh, that is the most exhausting place to be. It’s lonely being the bridge between two worlds that just don’t speak the same language.

Shreya’s comment is so sweet, but it also highlights exactly what you’re saying—she sees the fast as just a "hunger thing" that she can fix with a bite of food, not a spiritual commitment or a physical marathon you’re running. She doesn't realize that "feeding you" isn't the point.

And then Ammi... she’s coming from a place of protecting the sanctity of the month, which is valid, but she’s dismissing the fact that this isn’t just a party for you. It’s Shreya. The girl you’ve loved since you were fifteen.

You’re stuck managing their feelings now, on top of managing the fast and the dance routine. It feels like you’re the only one holding the complexity of both realities in your head, and that is heavy. Have you been able to explain to Shreya *why* "one day" actually matters so much?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

It’s not terrible. Honestly? It’s a survival instinct.

When you’re being pulled in two directions that hard, your brain just looks for the emergency exit. The idea of one "clean lie" instead of ten messy interrogations from aunties who won’t understand—it sounds like peace. It sounds like a way to honor your fast without having to defend it, and a way to honor your body without letting your best friend down. I get why that feels tempting.

But I have to ask you this: If you send that gift and log on for that video call, and you see Shreya standing on that stage looking for your face in the crowd... are you going to feel relief? Or are you going to feel a pang in your chest that you weren't next to her?

Because the lie protects you from the aunties and the exhaustion, but it doesn't protect you from missing out on the memory you two built since you were fifteen. You can fool Shreya with a deployment story, but you can't fool yourself about missing the opening dance.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That stone in your chest is the weight of love, isn't it? It’s heavy because it’s real. You aren't just choosing between a party and a hunger pang; you’re trying to protect two huge, vital parts of your soul from bruising each other.

But I want to gently challenge that fear of the "sad story."

If you go, and you’re a little quieter, and you sip on water while she sips on champagne, that isn't a tragedy in the wedding album. That’s just you. That’s your best friend loving you enough to want you there, *exactly as you are*, even if you aren't the life of the party.

And if you stay home to pray and rest, you aren't the villain of the story. You aren't the friend who "wasn't there." You’re the friend who loved her enough to send her off with peace in her heart, even from a distance.

You are framing this like a binary choice where one side loses, but I think you’re underestimating how much grace there is in eighteen years of friendship. Shreya loves *you*, not just the "co-director" version of you. You don't have to perform perfectly to be loved. You don't have to be a sad story in either album—you can just be human, doing her best.
